The heart of the word angular is the word angle — a sharp corner or point where two lines or edges meet. So when something is described as angular, the basic idea is: it has sharp corners, hard edges, or a pointed quality rather than being smooth, curved, or rounded.

Think of the difference between a circle and a triangle. The circle is smooth and curved all the way around — nothing sharp. The triangle has three distinct corners, three hard edges. The triangle is angular. The circle is not.

That one core idea — sharpness, pointedness, hard edges — branches out into several related meanings depending on what you're describing.
Meaning 1: Describing Shapes and Physical Objects

When you describe a shape, object, or structure as angular, you mean it has clear, sharp corners and straight, hard edges rather than gentle curves or soft rounded surfaces.

  • A box is angular. A ball is not.
  • Modern architecture — think of buildings with sharp geometric lines, flat surfaces, and hard corners — is often described as angular. A dome or an arch is not.
  • A crystal with flat faces and sharp edges is angular. A smooth river pebble worn down by water is not.
  • A person's jawline can be angular — meaning it is strongly defined, sharp, and hard-edged rather than soft and rounded.

The key test: if you ran your eye (or finger) along it, would you hit a sudden, sharp corner? Or would it glide smoothly without interruption? Sharp corners = angular.
Meaning 2: Describing a Person's Body or Face

When used to describe a person's physical appearance, angular means they are thin, with prominent, sharp-looking bones visible beneath the skin — giving their face or body a bony, hard-edged quality.

An angular face typically has:

  • High, sharp cheekbones
  • A strongly defined jawline
  • A prominent, pointed chin
  • Little soft flesh to round out the features

An angular body is lean and bony — think of sharp shoulder blades, clearly visible collar bones, elbows that look pointy rather than smooth.

The reason this connects to the core meaning is simple: when there is little fat or flesh to soften and round out the body, the underlying bone structure shows through — and bones create edges, corners, and angles. A well-fed, rounded face softens those edges. An angular face does not have that softening.

Example: "She had an angular face — all sharp cheekbones and a defined jaw — that made her look striking but severe."

When used to describe how someone moves or behaves, angular means stiff, jerky, and lacking smooth grace or flow. The movements have sudden, rigid changes of direction — like a shape made of sharp corners — rather than being fluid and easy.

Think of how a dancer or an athlete might move in a smooth, flowing, curved path — graceful and continuous. Now imagine someone whose movements are stiff and robotic, changing direction suddenly and sharply, without any smooth transition. That second person moves in an angular way.

This meaning extends to personality and manner too. A person who is angular in their manner or behavior comes across as stiff, blunt, and a little awkward — lacking the smooth social ease and warmth that makes interaction feel effortless. They may be direct to the point of being sharp, without the softer, rounded edges of tact or charm.

Example: "His angular gestures while speaking made him seem nervous and rigid."
Example: "She had an angular personality — brilliant, but blunt and a little uncomfortable to be around."

In science, mathematics, and physics, the word angular is used in a precise technical way. It simply means "relating to, or involving an angle." This is the most literal use of the word, and it appears in specific technical phrases:

  • Angular velocity: How fast something is rotating — how quickly it sweeps through an angle. A spinning top has angular velocity.
  • Angular momentum: A measure of how much rotational motion an object has. A spinning figure skater has angular momentum.
  • Angular distance / angular size: In astronomy, the size or distance of an object as measured by the angle it takes up in your field of view, rather than its actual physical size. The Moon and the Sun look the same angular size in the sky (which is why solar eclipses work), even though the Sun is vastly larger in reality.

You don't need to master these scientific concepts fully right now, but it is useful to know that whenever you see angular used in a science or math context, it is simply asking: "what is the angle involved here?"
How All the Meanings Fit Together

All four meanings trace back to the same root idea — the quality of having angles: sharpness, hard edges, sudden corners, and the absence of softness or smoothness.

Movement & personalityStiff, rigid, lacking smooth grace

Putting It All Together With Examples

• "The angular lines of the new skyscraper made it stand out among the older, rounded buildings nearby." → Sharp-cornered, hard-edged design.
  • "He had an angular face, all sharp planes and edges, with cheekbones like a knife." → Bony, prominent features.
  • "Her dancing was angular and abrupt — lacking the fluid grace the judges were looking for." → Stiff, jerky, lacking flow.
  • "The satellite's angular velocity increased as it dropped closer to Earth." → The rate at which its angle of rotation changed.

The clearest opposite of angular is rounded or curvaceous — smooth, soft, flowing, without sharp corners or hard edges. Understanding the opposite often cements the meaning of a word firmly in your mind. Whenever you're unsure whether something is angular, ask yourself: is this smooth and rounded, or is this sharp-cornered and hard-edged? If it's the latter, angular is your word.
